claim: Most neutrophils transmigrate at the first cell-cell junction they encounter under flow conditions.
source: Using transendothelial migration (TEM) under flow assays (Heemskerk et al., 2016), we observed that although most neutrophils transmigrated at the first cell-cell junction they encounter (Figure 1A), only half of them transmigrated immediately upon arrival to that junction (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1A and experimental observations under flow conditions.

claim: Only half of neutrophils transmigrate immediately upon arrival at the first junction.
source: Using transendothelial migration (TEM) under flow assays (Heemskerk et al., 2016), we observed that although most neutrophils transmigrated at the first cell-cell junction they encounter (Figure 1A), only half of them transmigrated immediately upon arrival to that junction (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B from TEM under flow assays.

claim: Approximately 40% of neutrophils change direction upon diapedesis, migrating underneath the endothelial cell they previously crawled on.
source: In fact, approximately 40% of these neutrophils changed direction upon diapedesis, meaning that once arrived at the cell-cell junction, these neutrophils migrated on top of that junction, turned around and exited by migrating underneath the endothelial cell that they previously crawled on (Figure 1C), in line with Schenkel et al., 2004.
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1C and consistent with previous findings by Schenkel et al., 2004.

claim: Under physiological flow conditions, most neutrophils search for specific sites on the endothelium to exit.
source: The findings presented here confirm that under physiological flow conditions, most neutrophils search for specific sites on the endothelium to exit (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations under flow conditions shown in video.

claim: Endothelial cells display junctional membrane protrusions (JMPs) that extend apically into the lumen.
source: 3D reconstructions revealed that the endothelium extended membrane protrusions apically into the lumen (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by 3D reconstruction images from lattice light sheet microscopy.

claim: JMPs show a highly dynamic appearance and various morphological shapes, ranging from finger-like to flap-like structures.
source: These protrusions showed a highly dynamic appearance and various morphological shapes, ranging from finger-like to flap-like structures and are not restricted to one junction (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: Supported by video observations of JMP morphology.

claim: Long-term TNFα treatment (20 hr) increases the overall volume of JMPs.
source: These data revealed that short-term, that is, 4 hr (not shown), and long-term TNFα treatment, that is, 20 hr, to the same extend increased the overall volume of the JMPs as well as the dynamics of these JMPs, as well as the area of the JMP on the endothelium, although the latter one was not significant (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E-F using LLSM imaging and automated analysis.

claim: TNFα treatment increases the dynamics of JMPs.
source: These data revealed that short-term, that is, 4 hr (not shown), and long-term TNFα treatment, that is, 20 hr, to the same extend increased the overall volume of the JMPs as well as the dynamics of these JMPs, as well as the area of the JMP on the endothelium, although the latter one was not significant (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E-F demonstrating increased fluctuations in JMP volume over time.

claim: JMPs colocalize with VE-cadherin.
source: Figure 1G shows an example of such a JMP dynamics in time map and showed that JMPs colocalized with VE-cadherin (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing colocalization in Figure 1G-H.

claim: All inflammatory stimuli tested (TNFα, LPS, IFNγ, and IL1β) show the same JMP dynamics.
source: We additionally checked if other inflammatory stimuli, that is, LPS, INFγ, and IL1β, changed the dynamic rate of JMPs compared to TNFα. Using the simplified algorithm to generate a membrane dynamics map, we quantified JMPs by simply taking the mean value of this image (for details see Materials and methods section). We found that all inflammatory stimuli tested showed the same JMP dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing different inflammatory stimuli shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: JMP dynamics do not differ in endothelial cells isolated from different origins.
source: Also, when we tested JMP dynamics in endothelial cells that were isolated from different origin, we did not find differences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing endothelial cells from different origins shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Short-term flow (5 or 20 min) increases JMP activity.
source: Indeed, short-term flow for 5 or 20 min did increase JMP activity, whereas exposure of the endothelial cells to longer periods of flow, that is, 30–60 min, reduced JMP dynamics back to basal levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing increased JMP dynamics with short-term flow in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Longer periods of flow (30-60 min) reduce JMP dynamics back to basal levels.
source: Indeed, short-term flow for 5 or 20 min did increase JMP activity, whereas exposure of the endothelial cells to longer periods of flow, that is, 30–60 min, reduced JMP dynamics back to basal levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics with longer flow exposure in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is no preference of JMP dynamics at the upstream or downstream side of the flow direction.
source: We did not find any preference of JMP dynamics at the upstream or downstream side of the flow direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing upstream and downstream JMP dynamics in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inflammatory stimuli promote the dynamics but not the actual appearance or size of JMPs.
source: Thus, these data show that inflammatory stimuli promote the dynamics but not the actual appearance or size of JMPs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments testing different inflammatory stimuli and their effects on JMP characteristics.

claim: Most neutrophils prefer exit-sites with high-membrane activity.
source: To investigate this, mNeonGreen-CAAX transduced HUVECs were used to study neutrophil TEM under flow conditions. We found that most neutrophils preferred exit-sites with high-membrane activity (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and quantification shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: JMP dynamics are increased at sites where neutrophils transmigrate compared to sites where neutrophils migrate along the junction but do not exit.
source: In line with the idea that neutrophils preferred JMPs, we found that JMP dynamics were increased at sites where neutrophils transmigrated compared to sites where neutrophils migrated along the junction but did not exit (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing JMP dynamics at different sites shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Neutrophils prefer to initiate diapedesis by crawling towards a JMP of the neighboring endothelial cell.
source: Moreover, we found that neutrophils preferred to initiate diapedesis by crawling towards a JMP of the neighboring endothelial cell. Consequently, the neutrophil used this JMP to exit and continued crawling underneath the endothelial cell that generated the JMP (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data showing neutrophil behavior at JMPs in Figure 2D and supplemental figures.

claim: Once a neutrophil uses a JMP to cross the endothelium, other neutrophils follow this path and use the same exit-site.
source: Interestingly, we observed that once a neutrophil used a JMP to cross the endothelium, other neutrophils followed this path and used the same exit-site (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by 3D imaging data showing sequential neutrophil transmigration at the same site in Figure 2E.

claim: Endothelial JMP dynamics increase at exit-sites after the first neutrophil crosses.
source: This was in line with an increase in endothelial JMP dynamics at exit-sites after the first neutrophil crossed (Figure 2F), in line with a recent publication by Hyun et al., 2019.
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing increased JMP dynamics after transmigration in Figure 2F and consistent with published findings.

claim: Endothelial JMPs can function as exit-recognition sites that are reinforced by transmigration.
source: These data suggest that endothelial JMPs can function as exit-recognition sites that are reinforced by transmigration.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from observations that JMP dynamics increase after transmigration and subsequent neutrophils use the same sites.

claim: VE-cadherin localizes at the basolateral area of JMPs but is not present on the actual JMP.
source: To study the JMP phenotype in more detail, we used LLSM imaging and found that VE-cadherin localized at the basolateral area of JMPs but is not present on the actual JMP (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing VE-cadherin localization in Figure 3A.

claim: Junctional PECAM-1/CD31 is present on JMPs.
source: In contrast, junctional PECAM-1/CD31 was present on JMPs (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing PECAM-1 localization on JMPs in Figure 3B and supplemental figure.

claim: PECAM-1 covers at least 50% of the surface of the JMP.
source: Using a 3D quantification algorithm, we found that PECAM-1 covered at least 50% of the surface of the JMP (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data from 3D analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PECAM-1-rich membrane protrusions can be found in vivo in the cremaster muscle of mice.
source: To examine whether JMPs are found in vivo and are correlated to TEM events, we used the cremaster muscle as a well-established in vivo model. The cremaster muscle of C57BL/6 mice were treated with TNF/IL1β and subsequently stained for PECAM-1 and neutrophil-specific coronin1 (Pick et al., 2017). We found that PECAM-1-rich membrane protrusions can also be found in vivo, although we cannot quantify them as JMPs based on these images.
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data from cremaster muscle shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PECAM-1 covers apical protrusions that surround adherent neutrophils in vivo.
source: As with the in vitro data, PECAM-1 covered the apical protrusions that surrounded adherent neutrophils in vivo (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data showing PECAM-1 coverage around neutrophils in Figure 3D.

claim: ACKR1 is expressed at CAAX-identified JMPs.
source: To examine the location of ACKR1, we expressed an mNeonGreen-tagged variant of ACKR1 in HUVECs together with mScarlet-I-CAAX to label the membrane and cultured the cells in a mosaic manner to a full monolayer. We observed that ACKR1 is expressed at CAAX-identified JMPs (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C), suggesting that chemokines can be presented by JMPs.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing ACKR1 localization at JMPs in Figure 3E and supplemental figures.

claim: ICAM-1 localizes to JMPs.
source: To identify the role of JMPs in the adhesion stage of TEM, we co-expressed ICAM-1 mScarlet-I and mNeonGreen-CAAX in HUVECs. Like ACKR1, ICAM-1 localized to JMPs (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing ICAM-1 localization at JMPs in Figure 3F and supplemental figures.

claim: ICAM-1 and ACKR1 are not enriched at JMPs.
source: Interestingly, when measuring the fluorescence at JMPs using a profile plot, we found that fluorescence of the proteins detected at JMPs increased to the same extend as the membrane marker CAAX (Figure 3—figure supplements 1B and D). Based on these data, we concluded that ICAM-1 and ACKR1 are not enriched at JMPs.
evidence: Supported by quantification of fluorescence intensity showing proportional increase with membrane marker in supplemental figures.

claim: JMPs may be involved in presenting ACKR1 as a chemokine presenter to crawling leukocytes.
source: These results suggest that JMPs may be involved in two key steps of TEM. First by presenting ACKR1 as a chemokine presenter to the crawling leukocytes (Pruenster et al., 2009) and second, by presenting endothelial cell adhesion molecules for the leukocyte integrins to start diapedesis.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from ACKR1 localization at JMPs and its known role in chemokine presentation, supported by citation.

claim: JMPs may be involved in presenting endothelial cell adhesion molecules for leukocyte integrins to start diapedesis.
source: These results suggest that JMPs may be involved in two key steps of TEM. First by presenting ACKR1 as a chemokine presenter to the crawling leukocytes (Pruenster et al., 2009) and second, by presenting endothelial cell adhesion molecules for the leukocyte integrins to start diapedesis.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from ICAM-1 localization at JMPs and its known role in leukocyte adhesion.

claim: JMPs are rich in F-actin.
source: To study the role of the actin cytoskeleton in JMPs, we used LifeAct-expressing endothelial cells and LLSM imaging, which revealed that JMPs are rich in F-actin (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing LifeAct signal at JMPs in Figure 4A.

claim: Actin-rich vascular structures that protrude apically are associated with TEM events in vivo.
source: To investigate if these structures are also present in vivo, we used Lifeact-GFP knock-in mice (Fraccaroli et al., 2012) and studied the inflamed cremaster muscle vessel morphology. As Lifeact-EGFP is mainly expressed in the vascular endothelium and not in the leukocytes, allowing imaging of the endothelial actin cytoskeleton with excellent contrast (Fraccaroli et al., 2012), we used these mice to study the presence of luminal membrane protrusions. In vivo time lapse imaging showed actin-rich vascular structures that protruded apically and were associated with TEM events (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by in vivo imaging data from Lifeact-GFP mice showing actin-rich protrusions during TEM in Figure 4B.

claim: Treatment of endothelial cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 reduces JMP dynamics.
source: As the Arp2/3 complex is involved in actin nucleation, branching and lamellipodia formation (Goley and Welch, 2006), we hypothesized that its activity is required for the dynamics of JMPs. Indeed, treatment of endothelial cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666 reduced JMP dynamics (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics after CK-666 treatment in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Silencing Arp3 in endothelial cells results in reduced number of neutrophils that cross the endothelial monolayer under flow conditions.
source: Therefore, we silenced Arp3 in endothelial cells using shRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 4—source data 1). Indeed, silencing Arp3, with two independent shRNAs, resulted in reduced number of neutrophils that crossed the endothelial monolayer under flow conditions (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced TEM events in Arp3-silenced cells in Figure 4E and supplemental figure.

claim: Endothelial cells silenced for Arp3 show reduced JMP dynamics.
source: To specifically quantify membrane dynamics in Arp3-deficient endothelial cells, we co-expressed the Arp3 shRNA and mNeonGreen-CAAX from one plasmid, assuring that CAAX-expressing cells were indeed silenced for Arp3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E). Endothelial cells that were silenced for Arp3 showed reduced JMP dynamics (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics in Arp3-silenced cells in Figure 4F and supplemental figure.

claim: Actin nucleation by the Arp2/3 complex is important for JMP formation and neutrophil TEM.
source: These data underscore the importance of actin nucleation by the Arp2/3 complex for JMP formation and neutrophil TEM.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing that Arp2/3 inhibition or silencing reduces both JMP dynamics and neutrophil TEM.

claim: Rac1 inhibitor (EHT1864) reduces JMP dynamics.
source: To test if Rac1 is required for JMPs, we used a Rac1 inhibitor (EHT1864) and found that JMP dynamics were reduced (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing reduced JMP dynamics after EHT1864 treatment in Figure 5A and supplemental figure.

claim: JMPs display a significant increase in Rac1 activation.
source: Next, we used FRET-based DORA Rac1 biosensor to measure Rac1 activity at JMPs (Timmerman et al., 2016; Timmerman et al., 2015). To this end, endothelial cells were transfected with the Rac1 biosensor and with mScarlet-I-CAAX. The FRET ratio was used as a read-out of Rac1 activity, and it was measured at JMP regions and compared with the average ratio at the full cell junctional region (for details see Materials and methods section). This analysis showed that JMPs displayed a significant increase in Rac1 activation (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by FRET-based biosensor measurements showing increased Rac1 activity at JMPs in Figure 5B-C and supplemental figures.

claim: Neutrophils prefer to cross the endothelium at sites with high FRET ratio (high Rac1 activity).
source: To correlate Rac1 activation with neutrophil diapedesis, we mapped the areas where neutrophils crossed the endothelium to the FRET ratio of the Rac1 biosensor. We found that neutrophils preferred to cross the endothelium at sites with high FRET ratio (Figure 5D–E and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing neutrophils crossing at high Rac1 activity sites in Figure 5D-E and video.

claim: No change in Rac1 activity is detected at regions where neutrophils adhere and crawl on the surface of the endothelium.
source: However, no change in Rac1 activity was detected at regions where neutrophils adhered and crawled on the surface of the endothelium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that the adhesion and lateral migration of neutrophils themselves did not trigger Rac1 activity in endothelial cells.
evidence: Supported by FRET measurements showing no change in Rac1 activity under crawling neutrophils in supplemental figures.

claim: JMPs depend on Rac1 activity.
source: Together, these findings reveal that JMPs depend on Rac1 activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing that Rac1 inhibition reduces JMP dynamics and that JMPs show increased Rac1 activity.

claim: Local JMPs have an asymmetric phenotype at junction regions, with one cell generating the protrusion while the neighboring cell does not.
source: At this point, the contribution of the two neighboring endothelial cells to the JMP is unclear. To study individual, neighboring endothelial cells in more detail, we mixed HUVECs expressing either mNeonGreen-CAAX or mScarlet-I-CAAX. Mosaic-like expression enabled us to distinguish individual endothelial cells that were adjacent to one another (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). Interestingly, LLSM showed the presence of asymmetrical JMPs, meaning that one cell generated the protrusion, while the neighboring cell did not (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by LLSM imaging data showing asymmetric JMPs in mosaic-labeled cells in Figure 6A and supplemental figures.

claim: Scanning electron microscopy confirms that JMPs display an asymmetric phenotype at endothelial cell-cell junction regions.
source: Using scanning electron microscopy, we confirmed that JMPs displayed an asymmetric phenotype at endothelial cell-cell junction regions (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by scanning electron microscopy images showing asymmetric JMPs in Figure 6B and supplemental figure.

claim: One endothelial cell shows higher JMP dynamics compared to the adjacent one at junction regions.
source: To quantify this, we analyzed membrane dynamics at JMP regions using mosaic-expressing endothelial cells and found that one endothelial cell showed higher JMP dynamics compared to the adjacent one, as indicated by a ratio >1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing asymmetric JMP dynamics between adjacent cells in Figure 6C.

claim: The active Tiam1 mutant, C1199, activates endogenous Rac1 in endothelial cells.
source: To further assess if local Rac1 activation can trigger the direction of neutrophil transmigration across an asymmetric junction, we overexpressed the Rac-specific RhoGEF Tiam1 in endothelial cells. Biochemical analysis showed that the active Tiam1 mutant, C1199, activated endogenous Rac1 in endothelial cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by biochemical Rac1 pulldown assay data shown in supplemental figure.

claim: Tiam1-C1199 localizes at junctions as determined by VE-cadherin staining.
source: Additional immunofluorescence imaging revealed that Tiam1 localized at junctions as determined by a perpendicular line scan across the cell-cell junction indicated by VE-cadherin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and line scan analysis shown in supplemental figures.

claim: Tiam-C1199 recruits F-actin to junction sites.
source: Similar line scan analysis showed that Tiam-C1199 recruited F-actin to these sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G), in line with previous work by Lampugnani and co-workers (Lampugnani et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by line scan analysis showing increased F-actin at junctions in Tiam1-expressing cells in supplemental figure, consistent with published findings.

claim: Endothelial cells expressing Tiam1-C1199 show increased F-actin content at junction regions.
source: Where endothelial cells that expressed only control plasmids showed low levels of F-actin at junction regions, endothelial cells that showed asymmetric expression of Tiam1 (meaning one cell expressed Tiam1 and the adjacent cell did not) or both endothelial cells expressed Tiam1 showed increased F-actin content at junction regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: Supported by quantification of F-actin staining at junctions shown in supplemental figures.

claim: Tiam1-C1199-induced junctional protrusions are approximately 2.5 µm in height.
source: Tiam1-C1199-induced junctional protrusions were approximately 2.5 µm in height, as was determined by 3D imaging (Figure 6D) and were reduced in height upon treatment with the Rac1 inhibitor EHT1864 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by 3D imaging measurements shown in Figure 6D and supplemental figure.

claim: Neutrophils prefer to migrate underneath a Tiam1-C1199 expressing cell.
source: When measuring the direction of migrating neutrophils that crossed the endothelium, we observed that neutrophils preferred to migrate underneath a Tiam1-C1199 cell (Figure 6E and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of neutrophil transmigration direction shown in Figure 6E and video.

claim: Neutrophils prefer to transmigrate underneath cells expressing constitutively active Rac1-Q61L.
source: Similar results were found when expressing the constitutive active variant of Rac1, Rac1-Q61L, in a mosaic manner with control cells expressing LifeAct (Figure 6F and Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: Supported by quantification of neutrophil transmigration direction in Rac1-Q61L expressing cells shown in Figure 6F and video.

claim: Neutrophils prefer to transmigrate across junctions that display an asymmetric protrusion on one of the two neighboring endothelial cells.
source: These data show that neutrophils prefer to transmigrate across junctions that display an asymmetric protrusion on one of the two neighboring endothelial cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with Tiam1-C1199 and Rac1-Q61L showing directional preference of neutrophil transmigration.

claim: Neutrophils migrate from the top of an 'inactive' cell to underneath the 'active' protruding endothelial cell.
source: As a result, neutrophils migrate from the top of an 'inactive' cell to underneath the 'active' protruding endothelial cell.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of neutrophil transmigration direction in asymmetric junctions.

claim: Local activation of photoactivatable Rac1 induces local membrane protrusions.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesized that local activation of Rac1, that is, one endothelial cell but not the neighboring one, triggers asymmetric JMPs that function as a local recognition site to drive diapedesis for neutrophils. To test this hypothesis, we used a genetically encoded photoactivatable Rac1 probe (Wu et al., 2009). By exciting the Lov2 domain, active Rac1 is released and induced local membrane protrusions (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing membrane protrusions upon blue light activation of PA-Rac1 in supplemental figures.

claim: Neutrophils prefer to transmigrate from the non-transfected cell underneath the PA-Rac1 expressing cell.
source: We found that neutrophils preferred to transmigrate in the direction from the non-transfected cell underneath the PA-Rac1 expressing cell, in line with data presented above (Figure 6G and Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: Supported by quantification of neutrophil transmigration direction with PA-Rac1 shown in Figure 6G and video.

claim: Local activation of the Rac1 probe increases the number of neutrophils that cross the endothelium.
source: Moreover, local activation of the Rac1 probe increased the number of neutrophils that crossed the endothelium (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing increased TEM events upon PA-Rac1 activation in Figure 6H and supplemental figure.

claim: Neutrophils prefer to exit the endothelium through junctions that display JMPs in an asymmetric manner.
source: In summary, our data indicate that neutrophils preferred to exit the endothelium through junctions that display JMPs in an asymmetric manner, meaning that one endothelial cell exposes an apical protrusion and the other one does not (Figure 6I).
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing asymmetric JMPs and directional neutrophil transmigration.

claim: Asymmetric JMP sites can be recognized as local endothelial TEM hotspots.
source: These sites can be recognized as local endothelial TEM hotspots.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations that neutrophils preferentially use asymmetric JMP sites for transmigration.

claim: Leukocytes use preferred exit sites during transmigration across the endothelium.
source: Upon inflammation, leukocytes rapidly transmigrate across the endothelium to enter the inflamed tissue. Evidence accumulates that leukocytes use preferred exit sites, alhough it is not yet clear how these hotspots in the endothelium are defined and how they are recognized by the leukocyte.
evidence: Statement based on accumulated evidence in the field, though specific mechanism was unclear prior to this study.

claim: Leukocytes prefer endothelial membrane protrusions at cell junctions for transmigration.
source: Using lattice light sheet microscopy, we discovered that leukocytes prefer endothelial membrane protrusions at cell junctions for transmigration.
evidence: Main finding of the study supported by LLSM imaging and multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Junctional membrane protrusions are present in an asymmetric manner, with one endothelial cell showing the protrusion and the adjacent one not.
source: Phenotypically, these junctional membrane protrusions are present in an asymmetric manner, meaning that one endothelial cell shows the protrusion and the adjacent one does not.
evidence: Key finding supported by LLSM and SEM imaging of mosaic-labeled endothelial cells.

claim: Leukocytes cross the junction by migrating underneath the protruding endothelial cell.
source: Consequently, leukocytes cross the junction by migrating underneath the protruding endothelial cell.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of neutrophil transmigration direction at asymmetric JMPs.

claim: JMPs depend on Rac1 activity.
source: These protrusions depend on Rac1 activity and by using a photo-activatable Rac1 probe, we could artificially generate local exit-sites for leukocytes.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing Rac1 inhibition reduces JMPs and PA-Rac1 activation induces JMPs and increases TEM.

claim: Local induced junctional membrane protrusions facilitate/steer leukocyte escape/exit from inflamed vessel walls.
source: Overall, we have discovered a new mechanism that uses local induced junctional membrane protrusions to facilitate/steer the leukocyte escape/exit from inflamed vessel walls.
evidence: Overall conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Leukocyte transendothelial migration comprises leukocyte rolling, arrest, crawling, firm adhesion, and diapedesis.
source: The current paradigm of leukocyte transendothelial migration (TEM) comprises leukocyte rolling, arrest, crawling, firm adhesion, and diapedesis (Alon and van Buul, 2017; Butcher, 1991; Muller, 2016; Nourshargh and Alon, 2014; Springer, 1994; Vestweber, 2015).
evidence: Established paradigm in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: Diapedesis occurs either through the endothelial junctions (paracellular route) or through the endothelial cell body (transcellular route).
source: The latter step occurs either through the endothelial junctions, known as the paracellular route or through the endothelial cell body, called the transcellular route (Carman, 2009; Wittchen, 2009).
evidence: Established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: Some locations favor the migration of multiple leukocytes that breach the endothelium in rapid succession.
source: Interestingly, some locations seem to favor the migration of multiple leukocytes that breech the endothelium in rapid succession (Abtin et al., 2014).
evidence: Observation from published literature cited.

claim: Prior to exiting the circulation, leukocytes change their crawling morphology to a round appearance.
source: Prior to exiting the circulation, leukocytes change their crawling morphology to a round appearance, indicating that at exit-sites differential and local regulation is required (Shulman et al., 2009).
evidence: Observation from published literature cited.

claim: What determines where leukocytes take the exit remains elusive.
source: However, what determines where leukocytes take the exit remains elusive.
evidence: Statement of the knowledge gap that this study addresses.

claim: Perivascular macrophages can secrete chemokines that may cause local queues for neutrophil diapedesis in vivo.
source: Recently, it has been shown that perivascular macrophages can secrete chemokines that may cause local queues for neutrophil diapedesis in vivo (Abtin et al., 2014).
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: High surface levels of ICAM-1 induce a transition from paracellular to robust transcellular migration.
source: For example, high surface levels of ICAM-1 induce a transition from paracellular to robust transcellular migration, while intermediate levels favor the paracellular route (Abadier et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2005), although the underlying mechanism is unclear.
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: Intermediate levels of ICAM-1 favor the paracellular route of transmigration.
source: For example, high surface levels of ICAM-1 induce a transition from paracellular to robust transcellular migration, while intermediate levels favor the paracellular route (Abadier et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2005), although the underlying mechanism is unclear.
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: The endothelial actin cytoskeleton plays a dynamic role in controlling leukocyte TEM.
source: Data from our lab (Heemskerk et al., 2016; Timmerman et al., 2016; van Buul et al., 2007; van Buul et al., 2010) and that of others (Adamson et al., 1999; Barreiro et al., 2002; Barreiro et al., 2008; Carman and Springer, 2004; Lyck and Enzmann, 2015; Muller, 2015; Vestweber, 2015) indicate a dynamic role for the endothelial actin cytoskeleton in controlling the factors described above.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple studies from the authors' lab and others, supported by citations.

claim: Two different hotspots exist during extravasation in vivo, one of which is located on the endothelium.
source: Recently, Hyun and colleagues showed the existence of two different hotspots during extravasation in vivo (Hyun et al., 2019), one of which is located on the endothelium.
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: Blocking actin polymerization of the endothelium prevents the leukocyte from properly adhering and spreading, and critically impairs leukocyte TEM.
source: Perturbation of the endothelial actin cytoskeleton drastically influences the phenotype of the adherent leukocyte: blocking actin polymerization of the endothelium prevents the leukocyte to properly adhere and spread and consequently, leukocyte TEM is critically impaired (Barreiro et al., 2002; Carman et al., 2003; Carman and Springer, 2004; Schimmel et al., 2018; van Buul et al., 2010).
evidence: Finding from multiple published studies cited.

claim: Once a leukocyte has adhered to the endothelium, F-actin is locally depolymerized underneath the adherent leukocyte.
source: On the other hand, once a leukocyte has adhered to the endothelium, F-actin is locally (i.e. underneath the adherent leukocyte) depolymerized (Isac et al., 2011)
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: The endothelium can orchestrate local leukocyte diapedesis by remodeling its actin cytoskeleton at the subcellular level.
source: These findings suggest that the endothelium can orchestrate local leukocyte diapedesis by remodeling its actin cytoskeleton at the subcellular level.
evidence: Inference drawn from findings about actin polymerization and depolymerization during TEM.

claim: Leukocyte diapedesis is not a random event but occurs at predefined exit-sites.
source: Our observations underscore that leukocyte diapedesis is not a random event but occurs at predefined exit-sites.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the authors' observations throughout the study.

claim: Leukocytes cross the endothelium within 120 seconds.
source: As TEM is a very rapid process (leukocytes cross the endothelium within 120 s), we used lattice light sheet microcopy, allowing high-speed imaging in three dimensions in time with high resolution but low toxicity to monitor TEM in detail.
evidence: Observation about the timescale of TEM that motivated the use of LLSM.

claim: Lattice light sheet microscopy allows high-speed imaging in three dimensions in time with high resolution but low toxicity.
source: As TEM is a very rapid process (leukocytes cross the endothelium within 120 s), we used lattice light sheet microcopy, allowing high-speed imaging in three dimensions in time with high resolution but low toxicity to monitor TEM in detail.
evidence: Description of the technical capabilities of LLSM.

claim: JMPs express ACKR1, ICAM-1, and PECAM-1.
source: By asymmetrically inducing Rac1- and Arp3-dependent apical membrane protrusions at cell-cell junction regions that express ACKR1, ICAM-1, and PECAM-1, the endothelium guides leukocytes to the exit-side.
evidence: Summary of findings about molecular composition of JMPs.

claim: JMPs are found in vivo.
source: Additionally, these protrusions are also found in vivo, and local activation of Rac1, using a photo-activatable Rac1 probe drives leukocyte exit on demand.
evidence: Finding from in vivo experiments in cremaster muscle.

claim: Local activation of Rac1 using a photo-activatable Rac1 probe drives leukocyte exit on demand.
source: Additionally, these protrusions are also found in vivo, and local activation of Rac1, using a photo-activatable Rac1 probe drives leukocyte exit on demand.
evidence: Finding from PA-Rac1 experiments showing controlled induction of TEM.

claim: JMPs offer new therapeutic targets to locally inhibit or enhance leukocyte extravasation.
source: Our work identified so-called endothelial junctional membrane protrusions (JMPs), a novel molecular mechanism that allows local steering of leukocyte TEM at the vascular level and offers new therapeutic targets to locally inhibit or enhance leukocyte extravasation.
evidence: Speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: TEM hotspots exist and are particularly recognized in vivo.
source: Although there is consensus that so-called TEM hotspots exist, and are in particularly recognized in vivo (Proebstl et al., 2012; Hyun et al., 2019; Schimmel et al., 2017), it is unclear how such specific exit-spots are defined and regulated.
evidence: Statement of consensus in the field supported by citations.

claim: JMPs open the junctional cleft and serve as a trap for the crawling neutrophil.
source: Our data suggest that the JMPs open the junctional cleft and serve as a trap for the crawling neutrophil.
evidence: Interpretation of the mechanism by which JMPs function based on experimental observations.

claim: A local asymmetric protrusion at junction regions intercepts crawling neutrophils.
source: JMPs are induced on one endothelial cell whereas the adjacent one shows low lamella activity. Consequently, a local asymmetric protrusion at junction regions appears that intercepts crawling neutrophils (Figure 6I).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of asymmetric JMPs and neutrophil behavior.

claim: A unique mechanism is used by crawling immune cells to efficiently cross the inflamed endothelial barrier in a paracellular manner.
source: Thus, we have identified a unique mechanism that is used by crawling immune cells to efficiently cross the inflamed endothelial barrier in a paracellular manner.
evidence: Overall conclusion of the study based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: Local stiffness has been proposed to control TEM hotspots.
source: However, it has been a longstanding question in the field how such endothelial hotspots are regulated or what would characterize such hotspots. Many options have been proposed to mediate hotspots. For example, local stiffness has been proposed to control this, either induced by the substrate underneath the endothelium or by the endothelium itself by expressing local stiff actin-based structures (Martinelli et al., 2014; Schaefer et al., 2014).
evidence: Hypothesis from published literature cited.

claim: Local expression of adhesion molecules has been suggested as a key element for TEM hotspots.
source: Also local expression of adhesion molecules has been suggested as one of the key elements for such TEM hotspots (Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: Hypothesis from published literature cited.

claim: The display of chemokines at junctions has been an attractive hypothesis for the induction of local exit.
source: And recently, the display of chemokines at junctions has been an attractive hypothesis for the induction of local exit (Girbl et al., 2018; Pruenster et al., 2009; Thiriot et al., 2017).
evidence: Hypothesis from published literature cited.

claim: During TEM, endothelial-derived chemokines followed by neutrophil-derived chemokines are presented on the endothelial surface at junction regions with the help of ACKR1.
source: The work by Girbl and colleagues showed that during TEM, endothelial-derived chemokines followed by neutrophil-derived chemokines are presented on the endothelial surface, at junction regions with the help of ACKR1, to guide the neutrophils through.
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: Guiding molecules need JMPs for optimal exposure to crawling leukocytes to initiate diapedesis.
source: Our data add to this study by showing that JMPs express ACKR1, as well as ICAM-1 and PECAM-1. We propose that these guiding molecules need JMPs for optimal exposure to the crawling leukocytes to initiate diapedesis.
evidence: Proposal based on the authors' findings about molecular composition of JMPs.

claim: Local lamellipodia are involved in controlling the endothelial barrier function.
source: Many different types of membrane structures have been described to emerge in endothelial cells. Breslin and colleagues described local lamellipodia to be involved in controlling the endothelial barrier function (Breslin et al., 2015).
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: Local lamellipodia depend on Rac1 signaling and myosin-mediated local tension.
source: These structures depend on Rac1 signaling and myosin-mediated local tension and show great similarities to JMPs.
evidence: Finding from published literature about lamellipodia that shows similarities to JMPs.

claim: Membrane protrusions positive for PECAM-1 surround adhering and transmigrating leukocytes in vivo.
source: Membrane protrusions have also been detected in vivo. Such protrusions were found to be positive for PECAM-1 and surrounded adhering and transmigrating leukocytes (Petri et al., 2011; Phillipson et al., 2008).
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: Protrusions may function to prevent vascular leakage during leukocyte emigration.
source: These studies argued that the protrusions may function to prevent vascular leakage. Although we did not study if JMPs contribute to the limitation of vascyular leakge during leukocyte emigration, this is an attractive hypothesis.
evidence: Hypothesis from published literature that the authors did not test but consider plausible.

claim: This mechanism can function as a target for pharmacological blockers.
source: For therapeutic potential, not only can this mechanism now function as a target and pharmacological blockers can be developed, but more importantly, it may lead to novel strategies to initiate leukocyte traffic to parts of the body where we wish to have more immune cells present, for example for immune cell therapies.
evidence: Speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: This mechanism may lead to novel strategies to initiate leukocyte traffic to specific parts of the body for immune cell therapies.
source: For therapeutic potential, not only can this mechanism now function as a target and pharmacological blockers can be developed, but more importantly, it may lead to novel strategies to initiate leukocyte traffic to parts of the body where we wish to have more immune cells present, for example for immune cell therapies.
evidence: Speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: JMPs do not seem to be induced by leukocytes themselves, but rather through an intrinsic mechanism within the endothelium triggered by inflammation signals.
source: For the regulation aspect: it is important to note that JMPs do not seem to be induced by leukocytes themselves, but rather through an intrinsic mechanism within the endothelium triggered by inflammation signals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing JMP dynamics are not affected by crawling neutrophils.

claim: TNFα results in long-term activation of Rac1.
source: Indeed, TNFα results in long-term activation of Rac1 (Van Rijssel et al., 2013; Wójciak-Stothard et al., 1998).
evidence: Finding from published literature cited.

claim: Crawling leukocytes do not trigger the activity or dynamics of JMPs.
source: Our data does not support a model in which crawling leukocytes trigger the activity or dynamics of JMPs. When measuring JMP dynamics in the presence or absence of crawling leukocytes, we did not detect any difference in JMP activity.
evidence: Finding from experiments comparing JMP dynamics with and without crawling neutrophils.

claim: The localization of JMPs does not change when neutrophils are added.
source: Also, the localization of the JMPs did not change when neutrophils were added, and Rac1 activity did not change when leukocytes crawled on top of an endothelial cells.
evidence: Finding from experiments measuring JMP localization and Rac1 activity with crawling neutrophils.

claim: Rac1 activity does not change when leukocytes crawl on top of endothelial cells.
source: Also, the localization of the JMPs did not change when neutrophils were added, and Rac1 activity did not change when leukocytes crawled on top of an endothelial cells.
evidence: Finding from FRET measurements of Rac1 activity under crawling neutrophils.

claim: Neutrophils do not necessarily choose the site of highest Rac1 activation in an endothelial cell.
source: In addition, we noticed that neutrophils did not per se choose the site of highest Rac1 activation in an endothelial cell, presumably because the Rac1 activation itself cannot be sensed from a distance.
evidence: Observation from FRET experiments with interpretation about sensing limitations.

claim: A neutrophil continues to crawl over the endothelium until it encounters a local JMP, which is associated with high Rac1 activity, which is then used for diapedesis.
source: We hypothesize that a neutrophil continues to crawl over the endothelium until it encounters a local JMP, which is associated with high Rac1 activity, which is then used for diapedesis.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The regulation of JMPs happens in a stochastic manner.
source: We postulate that the regulation of JMPs happens in a stochastic manner, in line with previous reports showing the stochastic behavior of endothelial cell monolayers in early immune responses (Lipniacki et al., 2006) and expression of for example von Willebrand factor (Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: Hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and consistent with published findings about stochastic endothelial behavior.

claim: Long-term flow conditions do not affect JMP dynamics or distribution.
source: As endothelial cells are constantly exposed to flow conditions, we expected JMPs to be influenced by flow as well. To our surprise, we did not measure any differences in JMP dynamics or distribution in the absence or presence of long-term flow.
evidence: Finding from experiments testing the effect of long-term flow on JMPs.

claim: Endothelial cells drastically adjust their morphology to long-term flow conditions by polarizing in the direction of the flow with increased Rac1 activity at the upstream side.
source: This was somewhat surprising, as it is well known that endothelial cells drastically adjust their morphology to long-term flow conditions by polarizing in the direction of the flow with increased Rac1 activity at the upstream side of the endothelial cell (Kroon et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2013; Tzima et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge from published literature cited.

claim: The stochastic regulation of JMPs under inflammatory conditions is independent of any flow direction.
source: However, the stochastic regulation of JMPs under inflammatory conditions is independent of any flow direction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing no directional preference of JMPs under flow.

claim: JMPs are different from junction-associated intermittent lamellipodia (JAILs).
source: Furthermore, as JMPs localize specifically at intact junction regions, we believe that these structures are therefore per definition different from junction-associated intermittent lamellipodia (JAILs) that have been described previously (Cao et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with previously described structures based on localization and regulation differences.

claim: JAILs are regulated by VEGFR2 and local release of junctional tension.
source: JAILs are regulated by VEGFR2 and local release of junctional tension whereas JMPs are present as apical structures on top of VE-cadherin-positive junction regions, display several trafficking molecules and are regulated by inflammatory stimuli.
evidence: Comparison with JAILs based on published literature about JAILs and the authors' findings about JMPs.

claim: JMPs are present as apical structures on top of VE-cadherin-positive junction regions.
source: JAILs are regulated by VEGFR2 and local release of junctional tension whereas JMPs are present as apical structures on top of VE-cadherin-positive junction regions, display several trafficking molecules and are regulated by inflammatory stimuli.
evidence: Finding from imaging data showing JMP localization relative to VE-cadherin.

claim: JMPs display several trafficking molecules.
source: JAILs are regulated by VEGFR2 and local release of junctional tension whereas JMPs are present as apical structures on top of VE-cadherin-positive junction regions, display several trafficking molecules and are regulated by inflammatory stimuli.
evidence: Finding from imaging data showing ACKR1, ICAM-1, and PECAM-1 on JMPs.

claim: JMPs are regulated by inflammatory stimuli.
source: JAILs are regulated by VEGFR2 and local release of junctional tension whereas JMPs are present as apical structures on top of VE-cadherin-positive junction regions, display several trafficking molecules and are regulated by inflammatory stimuli.
evidence: Finding from experiments showing increased JMP dynamics with inflammatory stimuli.

claim: An endothelial membrane structure supports local exiting of crawling leukocytes.
source: In summary, we have identified an endothelial membrane structure that supports local exiting of crawling leukocytes.
evidence: Overall conclusion of the study.

claim: Whether JMPs are involved and perturbed in diseased conditions is not known but is an attractive hypothesis.
source: If these structures are also involved and perturbed in diseased conditions is not known but is an attractive hypothesis and would give new opportunities to target such pathologies.
evidence: Speculation about potential relevance to disease based on the findings.
